passages.original: Arcem : Josephus refert, hanc Petram 162 urbem nobilem Palaestinae.
passages.english: Arcem: Josephus reports that this is Petra, a famous city of Palestine.
passages.notes: The numeral 162 is an edition page/column marker and has been omitted. 'Arcem' is the headword (accusative form of 'arx', 'citadel'); the entry is evidently abridged.

passages.original: Babel, quae et Babylon, interpretatur confusio. Erat autem civitas regni Nemrod, in qua eorum qui aedificaverunt turrim, linguae divisae sunt, quo- rum principem Josephus Nemrod fuisse affirmat. Testem quoque ejus historiae, Sibyllam Graecam exhibens : « Locus, inquit, in quo turrim aedifica- vere, nunc appellatur Babylon, propter confusio- nem 166 sermonis eorum, qui altissimam turrim omni studio fabricabantur. Siquidem Hebraei con- fusionem BABEL vocant. » De hac turre, et diversi- tate linguarum scribit et Sibylla in hunc modum : « Cum ommes mortales una lingua uterentur, qui- dam ex his altissimam turrim aedificavere, coelum per eam cupientes scandere : dii vero turbines ventosque mittentes, evertere turrim, et propriam atque diversam unicuique tribuere linguam : unde urbem quoque appellari contigit Babylonem.
passages.english: Babel, which is also Babylon, is interpreted 'confusion'. It was a city of the kingdom of Nimrod, in which the languages of those who built the tower were divided; Josephus affirms that their leader was Nimrod. He also brings forward the Greek Sibyl as a witness to this history: "The place," he says, "in which they built the tower is now called Babylon, because of the confusion of the speech of those who were constructing a very high tower with all zeal. For the Hebrews call confusion BABEL." The Sibyl also writes about this tower and the diversity of languages in this way: "When all mortals used one language, some of them built a very high tower, wishing to climb up to heaven by it; but the gods, sending whirlwinds and winds, overturned the tower and gave to each one his own and a different language; whence it came about that the city too was called Babylon."
passages.notes: The numeral 166 is an edition marker and has been omitted. 'ommes' read as 'omnes'.

passages.original: Evila, ubi aurum purissimum (quod Hebraice dicitur zaab (DKy) et gemmae pretiosissimae, car- bunculus, smaragdusque nascantur. Est autem regio ad Orientem vergens, quam circumit de paradiso Phison egrediens : quem nostri, mutato nomine 8, Gangen vocant. Sed et unus de minori- bus Noe Evila dictus est, quem Josephus refert cum fratribus suis a flumine Cephene et regione Indiae, usque ad eum locum qui appellatur Hieria, possedisse. Sed et Ismael in solitudine Evila habi- tasse scribitur : quam ait sancta Scriptura esse in deserto Sur contra faciem AEgypti, et tendere usque ad terram Assyriorum.
passages.english: Havilah, where the purest gold (which in Hebrew is called zaab) and most precious gems, carbuncle and emerald, are produced. It is a region lying toward the East, which the Pishon, going out from paradise, encircles; our people, with a changed name, call it the Ganges. Also one of the lesser descendants of Noah was called Havilah; Josephus reports that he, with his brothers, possessed [the land] from the river Cephene and the region of India as far as the place called Hieria. It is also written that Ishmael lived in the wilderness of Havilah, which holy Scripture says is in the desert of Shur, opposite Egypt, and stretches as far as the land of the Assyrians.
passages.notes: The Hebrew in parentheses is garbled in the scan ('DKy'); the parenthesis is not closed in the text. The '8' after 'nomine' is a footnote mark. 'Cephene' is probably for Cophen (cf. p17707).

passages.original: 202 Euphrates, fluvius Mesopotamiae, in para- diso oriens. (Porro Sallustius 1 auctor certissimus asserit tam Tigris quam Euphratis in Armenia fontes demonstrari. Ex quo animadvertimus aliter de paradiso et fluminibus ejus intelligendum.) Ellasar, civitas regis Arioch.
passages.english: Euphrates, a river of Mesopotamia, rising in paradise. (But Sallust, a most reliable authority, asserts that the sources of both the Tigris and the Euphrates are pointed out in Armenia. From this we perceive that paradise and its rivers must be understood otherwise.) Ellasar, city of King Arioch.
passages.notes: '202' is an edition marker; '1' after Sallustius is a footnote mark.

passages.original: Jerusalem, in qua regnavit Adonibesec, et postea eam tenuere Jebusaei, e quibus et sortita vocabu- lum est, quos multo post tempore David extermi- nans, totius eam Judaeae provinciae metropolim fabricatus est : eo quod ibi locum templi emerit (et impensas structurae Salomoni filio dereliquerit : hanc esse Josephus refert), quae in Genesi scribitur Salem, sub rege Melchisedech. Fuit autem in tribu Benjamin.
passages.english: Jerusalem, in which Adoni-bezek reigned, and afterwards the Jebusites held it, from whom it also received its name; David, driving them out a long time later, made it the capital of the whole province of Judaea, because he bought the site of the temple there (and left the expenses of the building to his son Solomon). Josephus reports that this is the city which is written in Genesis as Salem, under King Melchizedek. It was in the tribe of Benjamin.
passages.notes: The parenthesis in the Latin awkwardly encloses 'hanc esse Josephus refert'; I have construed it with the following clause about Salem.

passages.original: Sennaar, campus Babylonis, in quo turris ex- structa est. Unde egressus Assur aedificavit Nine- rem. Meminit hujus loci Josephus in primo Anti- quitatum libro, ita scribens : « De campo qui in Babylonia regione vocatur Sennaar, narrat Hestiaeus historicus, dicens : Quidam sacerdotum profugi de templo Enyalii 2 Jovis sacra rapientes, in Sennaar campum Babyloniae pervenere.
passages.english: Shinar, the plain of Babylon, in which the tower was built. Going out from there, Asshur built Nineveh. Josephus mentions this place in the first book of the Antiquities, writing thus: "Concerning the plain which is called Shinar in the region of Babylonia, the historian Hestiaeus tells, saying: Certain of the priests, fugitives from the temple of Enyalian Jupiter, carrying off the sacred objects, came to the plain of Shinar in Babylonia.
passages.notes: 'Ninerem' read as 'Nineven' (Nineveh). '2' after Enyalii is a footnote mark.

passages.original: Sophera, mons orientis in India, juxta quem h? bitaverunt filii Jectan, filii Heber. Quos Josephus refert a Cophene flumine et Indiae regionibus usque ad id locorum pervenisse, ubi appellatur regio Hie- ria : sed et classis Salomonis per triennium hinc quaedam commercia deportabat.
passages.english: Sophera, a mountain of the East in India, near which lived the sons of Joktan, son of Eber. Josephus reports that they reached from the river Cophen and the regions of India as far as the place where the region is called Hieria; and Solomon's fleet also brought certain goods of trade from here every three years.
passages.notes: 'h? bitaverunt' read as 'habitaverunt'. 'per triennium' could also mean 'over three years'.

passages.original: Salem, civitas Sicimorum, quae est Sichem; sed et alia villa ostenditur usque in praesentem diem (juxta AEliam contra occidentalem plagam hoc no- mine; in octavo quoque lapide a Scythopoli in campo vicus Salumias appellatur : Josephus vero Salem esse affirmat (Antiqq. lib. I, cap, 11), in qua regnavit Melchisedec, quae postea dicta est Solyma, et ad extremum, Hierosolymae nomen ac- cepit.)
passages.english: Salem, a city of the Shechemites, which is Shechem; but another village is also pointed out to the present day by this name (near Aelia, on the western side; also at the eighth milestone from Scythopolis there is a village in the plain called Salumias; but Josephus affirms (Antiquities book I, chapter 11) that Salem is the city in which Melchizedek reigned, which was afterwards called Solyma, and finally received the name Jerusalem).
passages.notes: The opening parenthesis's extent is unclear in the edition.

passages.original: Tigris, fluvius de paradiso exiens, juxta Scri- pturae fidem, pergensque contra Assyrios : et post multos circuitus, ut vult Josephus 1, in mare Ru- brum influens. Vocatur autem hoc nomine pro- pter velocitatem, instar bestiae nimia pernicitate currentis.
passages.english: Tigris, a river going out from paradise, according to the testimony of Scripture, and going toward the Assyrians; and after many windings, as Josephus holds, flowing into the Red Sea. It is called by this name because of its swiftness, like a beast running with exceeding speed.
passages.notes: '1' after Josephus is a footnote mark.

passages.original: Tharsis, nude aurum Salomoni deferebatur : hanc putat Josephus Tarsum urbem esse Ciliciae. Porro juxta Ezechiel prophetam Carthago sentitor. Siqui- dem in eo loco, ubi apud Septuaginta Interpretes legimus Carthaginem, in Hebraeo scriptum habet Tharsis. Nonnulli Indiam putaverunt (et de hoc tam in libro Epistolarum (Epist.
passages.english: Tarshish, from where gold was brought to Solomon; Josephus thinks this is Tarsus, a city of Cilicia. But according to the prophet Ezekiel it is understood as Carthage. For in the place where we read 'Carthage' in the Septuagint translators, the Hebrew has 'Tarshish' written. Some have thought it India (and about this it has been said more fully both in the book of Letters (Letter
passages.notes: 'nude' read as 'unde'; 'sentitor' as 'sentitur'. The passage breaks off mid-parenthesis; it continues in the following text.

passages.original: Ur Chaldaeorum, ubi mortuus est Aram, frater Abrahae : cujus hodieque, sicut Josephus refert, tumulus ostenditur. (Et super hoc quid nobis vi- deatur in libris Hebraicarum Quoestionum plenius diximus.)
passages.english: Ur of the Chaldeans, where Aram, the brother of Abraham, died; whose tomb, as Josephus reports, is shown even today. (And what our view is on this we have stated more fully in the books of Hebrew Questions.)
passages.notes: 'Aram' stands where Genesis has Haran (Aran), Abraham's brother; presumably the same person.

passages.original: Verum si ad horum modo Patrum documenta Tabulam adumbrare oporteat, solisque eorum sit vestigiis insistendum, vix uniuscujusque regionis seorsim multas describas, unam quae simul universam Iv τύτ3|>, ut Eusebius loquitur, Palaestinam exhibeat, ne vix quidem. Nam quod cl. Relando pridem observa- tum est, Eusebius, ejusque interpres Hieronymus, in unaquaque regione terrae Israeliticae intervalla loco- rum ab urbe illius regionis praecipua definiunt : ipsam vero urbem, quo loco sita sit, dicere praetermittunt.
passages.english: But if one had to sketch a map only according to the evidence of these Fathers, and one had to rely on their traces alone, you could scarcely draw many [maps] of each region separately, and one that would show the whole of Palestine at once, 'in [its] outline', as Eusebius puts it, not even scarcely. For, as the distinguished Reland observed long ago, Eusebius and his translator Jerome, in each region of the land of Israel, define the distances of places from the principal city of that region, but omit to say where that city itself is situated.
passages.notes: The Greek 'Iv τύτ3|>' is garbled by the scan; probably a phrase of Eusebius such as ἐν τύπῳ ('in outline/diagram'). The rendering 'in [its] outline' is conjectural.

passages.original: Satis ex his duobus, quae adduximus, liquet, universae Palaestinae imaginem ad Eusebii ac Hieronymi ingenium ex hisce eorum monimentis, tametsi omnium longe luculentissimis, non posse delineari; sed quaedam necesse esse prius ex aliorum geographorum maxime veterum auctoritate constituere, quibus domum ipsa, quae in incerto apud Eusebium sive Hieronymum haerent, asserantur.
passages.english: From these two [points] that we have adduced it is clear enough that an image of the whole of Palestine cannot be drawn, according to the intent of Eusebius and Jerome, from these works of theirs, even though they are by far the clearest of all; but that certain things must first be established from the authority of other geographers, especially ancient ones, by which the very things that remain uncertain in Eusebius or Jerome may be settled.
passages.notes: 'domum' appears to be a scanning error, perhaps for 'demum' ('at last'); translated loosely as part of 'may be settled'.
